entries.title: Trump Administration Delays Iowa Lead Detonation to Wednesday
entries.summary: The administration said it would be investigating the contractor that runs the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for how it handled the lead explosives.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is again delaying the planned detonation of lead explosives in Iowa, this time to Wednesday, after widespread outcry from communities furious that they were not sufficiently warned about the possibility of a toxic lead plume.

The White House is expected to investigate how dangerous lead azide explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant were allowed to deteriorate to the point that they needed to be detonated, as well as launch a probe into the contractor that manages the plant, a source familiar with the situation told The Washington Sun.

American Ordnance, the contractor responsible for managing the explosives at the plant, and its inspectors discovered the deterioration in the lead in March 2026, according to EPA permitting documents and Army communications reviewed by The Sun.

The White House, led by President Donald Trump’s new chief of staff Stephen Miller, convened a team of agency leaders alongside the Homeland Security Council and National Security Council over the past 48 hours to discuss why the explosives had to be detonated and how to mitigate potential risks to the public, the source said. Senior White House officials only became aware of the issue Thursday, even though the Army has been planning how to deal with the problem for about six months.

The source requested anonymity to describe details of the unfolding situation.

The Army had already delayed its planned detonation of 68 barrels of degrading lead azide to Monday from the Friday original schedule, warning that was the latest possible date before the risks of an uncontrolled explosion became too great.

Sunday night, the Army posted to X that the detonation would occur Wednesday “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.”

“The Army and our interagency partners have been working around the clock to safeguard all Americans in the region,” the Army said in the post. “Additional details on this situation will be forthcoming. The health and safety of all Americans has and always will be our first priority.”

The administration said in court filings that cold temperatures will dramatically increase the chances that the lead azide — which has been degrading for months — could spontaneously explode, sparking a public panic over a lead dust plume spreading in the air above the Middletown plant.

The Army insisted in court filings over the weekend that the explosion could not be delayed past Tuesday, at the latest, because of the risks. While a federal court temporarily blocked the EPA permit authorizing the explosion, Justice Department attorneys warned that the Army would proceed with the detonation plan regardless of the judge’s ruling because it deemed the situation to be an emergency that merited operating without a permit.

The Army also revealed in court filings that it previously considered and then abandoned a plan to neutralize the lead azide with chemicals, warning that it would be too dangerous for anyone to try opening the lids of the barrels holding the lead in order to do the chemical treatment.

“So this was truly a choice between controlled or uncontrolled detonation,” the source familiar with the situation said. Now the discussion has moved on to how the government can put “as many mitigation measures in place as possible to protect the public.”

Public anxiety about the dangers of a lead plume escalated over the weekend with news of the pending explosion. An Army official familiar with the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter, told The Sun that the “exposure for the unmitigated worst case scenario here would be roughly equivalent to living in Los Angeles or New York City for three days in 1985.” Leaded gasoline was still in use at that time, making ambient lead exposure relatively quite high compared to today.

No amount of lead is safe to ingest, according to public health experts. Lead is a toxin that is especially dangerous to children, who are more sensitive to brain and nerve system damage.

Iowa officials, including Gov. Kim Reynolds, said they were only made aware of the Army’s plans to detonate the explosive one week ago, when the Army published maps showing a possible lead dust plume stretching across southeastern Iowa and into Illinois.

The Army increased the risk of an uncontrolled explosion in preparation for the original detonation date by removing the heavy metal bunker doors protecting the lead azide. Now those doors cannot be replaced, and the explosive is more vulnerable to swings in cold temperatures, The Sun previously reported.

“Unfavorable winds could increase the dispersion of lead dust into the community,” according to a DOJ filing in court. “An uncontrolled deportation of nearly five tons of primary explosive would endanger soldiers, contractors, and the surrounding communities, all without many of the protective measures meant to minimize the risks from the blast — harm that cannot be undone.”

Iowa environmental groups on Thursday sued the EPA — which permitted the detonation — in an effort to try to delay the scheduled explosion. The Army is not party to the suit.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘One of Our Own’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 23, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A memorial at VIDA, a loss at Audi Field and a daunting challenge at Northwest Stadium. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 7/10. A quick shower is possible but this is the last warm-ish day of the week. Enjoy it before temperatures tumble. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

Nearly two weeks after a deadly shooting left the Logan Circle community reeling, the streets outside of VIDA Fitness filled on Saturday afternoon for a memorial to honor victims.

Family members of James Stuart, the Metropole building manager killed inside the gym by resident Dr. Matt Lambert, sobbed and held each other in grief. Stuart’s niece, Aby Stocker, told reporters that although her family “was going through it,” they appreciated remembering her Uncle J’s bright spirit and sense of humor.

“I think of his laugh,” she said. “I hear his laugh a lot.”

Andrew Wilkinson came out to honor the friendship he had with Stuart. Although the two were “a little catty” initially, they became inseparable. Wilkinson remembered asking to stay with Stuart as he underwent chemotherapy. “Being my best friend, he didn't hesitate,” he said.

The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports that several attendees emphasized the need for gun control. Constance Freeman, a gun violence survivor and leader of D.C.’s chapter of Moms Demand Action, came to honor MDA member and shooting victim Susan Hamerski.

“That one of our own was injured, it's important for us to stand up and show up for her — as we do all victims of gun violence,” she said.

VIDA Fitness founder and CEO David von Storch expects the gym to reopen Tuesday.

VIDA memorial (5712x4284, AR: 1.33)




DEEP DIVE

Spirits were low Saturday, after the Washington Spirit’s NWSL championship match against the Kansas City Current ended in a heartbreaking 2-1 loss, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports.

“Obviously, this one hurts way worse than any of the other ones,” Trinity Rodman told reporters. “I don’t think you even have words in the moment. It’s too fresh.”

It was the team’s third straight championship loss, but fans had hoped this year would be different. It was the Spirit’s first championship played at home, in front of a hungry, sold-out crowd at Audi Field. The surge of fans marching to the stadium from The Wharf ahead of the game felt like a preemptive victory parade. Those who couldn’t score tickets crowded into neighboring bars, ready to flood the streets for a postgame celebration.

“This is the time, this is the night,” said one superfan, waiting to enter Audi.

They never got that moment. Still, supporters felt some consolation in just what a spectacle the night had been, and all in the service of women’s sports, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

“We used to play at a high school soccerplex in Maryland, now we sell out a stadium, like, every week,” said one fan, a D.C. resident of 25 years and season ticket holder. “I love seeing it.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

A push to bring a 10-cent refundable deposit for bottles and cans to D.C. is dead. The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports that the bottle-deposit bill introduced by Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau won’t be advancing this year, largely because of a multimillion-dollar lobbying blitz against it by the beverage industry and growing concerns within the D.C. Council over whether it would increase costs for retailers and consumers.

Some 10 states have bottle deposit programs in place; advocates say they increase recycling rates and could cut down on trash that ends up in D.C.-area rivers. Nadeau, who is leaving office in January, says she hopes a future council will take up the bill again.

The future of Montessori education in D.C. Public Schools is uncertain after the system allowed the accreditation for three schools to expire Friday. Shamira reports that J.C. Nalle and Langdon elementary schools and Capitol Hill Montessori at Logan will no longer be affiliated with the Association Montessori Internationale, the organization that sets international standards for many Montessori schools.

The decision comes after several parents have expressed surprise and concern over a changing curriculum. In a letter sent to parents days, DCPS said it plans to pursue accreditation from the American Montessori Society — another major Montessori organization — in a process that could take several years.

Out of the shadows: D.C. shadow Senator Ankit Jain is running for an at-large seat on the D.C. Council, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. Jain could retain his position as shadow senator while simultaneously serving on the council.

Monumental setback: A federal judge indefinitely suspended President Donald Trump’s plans to construct a 250-foot memorial arch in Arlington while a lawsuit brought by the county board plays out, Kendall reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

A Princeton doctoral student was arrested by ICE at Reagan National Airport last week as she prepared to fly back from a conference, NBC4 reports. The student, Eva Yi Xie, is being held at a detention center in Bowling Green.





FROM MARYLAND

The butterfly symbol that Maryland residents with hidden disabilities can feature on their state-issued IDs to have smoother interactions with first responders will be offered to students in Montgomery County Public Schools starting in January, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.





TRIVIA


How many teams were in the NWSL when the Spirit first joined in 2013?

  1. 8
  2. 10
  3. 12
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Dan Quinn AP - 26318716818509 (5070x3380, AR: 1.50)
The Commanders have their work cut out for them tonight. Hosting the Bengals on “Monday Night Football,” Washington will be tasked with finding a way to stop one of the league’s best offenses. But The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson reports that the team is undaunted, firm in its belief that they can compete with Joe Burrow and company.

“You can’t play this game, this position, having fear in your heart,” defensive back Amik Robertson said. “You respect the opponent, but you also go out there and play fearless.”

A lot of attention has been paid to Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa this season, but what about the rest of the team’s young core? As Washington struggles to get this season off the ground, The Sun’s Alex Schiffer checked in with scouts around the league to see how they view players like Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George and Tre Johnson.

What to Watch Today

NFL: Commanders vs. Bengals, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)
